items.html: Understand digital footprints and how to manage them
Follow net etiquette, communication etiquette and social media etiquette
Know about data protection and India's data protection law
Understand Intellectual Property Rights: copyright, patent, trademark
Recognise plagiarism and understand software licences (GPL, Apache, Creative Commons)
Identify cybercrimes and practise cyber safety
Know the main provisions of the IT Act, 2000
Understand e-waste and its safe disposal
Know the health effects of overusing technology

blocks.html: Technology has changed how we study, shop, pay, talk and work. A student in a Bihar village can attend an online class from IIT; a farmer can check crop prices on a phone. But technology also brings problems: fake news, online fraud, addiction and e-waste. A responsible user of the internet is called a netizen (net + citizen).
A digital footprint is the trail of data you leave behind when you use the internet.

rows: Posts, photos, comments, emails, online forms
Browsing history, location data, cookies, IP address, app usage

blocks.html: Your digital footprint is almost permanent. Colleges and employers may check it. Even deleted posts may have been saved as screenshots.

How to manage your digital footprint: Think before you post; set social media accounts to private; do not share personal details (address, phone, Aadhaar number) publicly; delete old unused accounts; clear browsing history and cookies; search your own name online sometimes.
(a) Net etiquette (netiquette) — good manners on the internet.

items.html: Be ethical: Do not copy others' work; respect copyright.
Be respectful: Respect privacy and different opinions; do not troll or bully.
Be responsible: Do not spread fake news; verify before forwarding.

blocks.html: (b) Communication etiquette — for email, chat and messages.

items.html: Be precise; write a clear subject line.
Be polite; avoid writing in ALL CAPS (it looks like shouting).
Do not send large attachments without asking; do not spam.
Respect people's time; avoid messaging late at night.
Choose a strong password and enable two-factor authentication.
Know who you befriend; do not accept requests from strangers.
Beware of fake information; check facts on reliable sources.
Think before uploading; once posted, it is hard to remove.

blocks.html: Data protection means keeping personal and sensitive data (bank details, health records, passwords, biometrics) safe from misuse, theft and unauthorised access.

items.html: Use strong passwords and do not reuse them.
Share only the data that is needed.
Check app permissions; a torch app does not need your contacts.
India passed the Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, 2023, which gives citizens rights over their personal data and requires companies to take consent and protect that data.

blocks.html: Intellectual property is a creation of the mind — an invention, a book, a song, a logo, software. IPR are the legal rights that protect such creations so the creator can benefit from them.

rows: Original creative work: books, music, films, software code, photos
The code of a mobile game; a textbook
A new medical device; a new method of water purification
A brand name, logo, symbol or slogan
The Tata logo; the Amul brand name

items.html: Plagiarism: Presenting someone else's work or ideas as your own without credit. Example: copying a project from the internet. Always cite your sources.
Copyright infringement: Using copyrighted work without permission, e.g. downloading pirated films or software.
Trademark infringement: Using another company's brand or logo without permission, e.g. fake branded shoes.

blocks.html: A software licence is a legal document that states how software may be used, copied and shared.

rows: Source code is secret; you pay to use it; cannot share
Free to use, modify and share, but changed versions must also be GPL ("copyleft")
Free to use and modify; changed versions can be closed source; must keep notices
For creative content (images, music, text); creator chooses conditions such as attribution (BY) or non-commercial (NC)

blocks.html: FOSS (Free and Open Source Software) — users can freely run, study, change and share the software. Examples: Linux, LibreOffice, Firefox, GIMP, the g++ compiler used in this book.
Cybercrime is any crime that uses a computer or the internet as a tool or a target.

rows: Breaking into a computer or account without permission
Fake emails, SMS or websites that trick you into giving passwords, OTPs or card details
Never share OTP/PIN; check the website address; banks never ask for OTP
Harassing, insulting or threatening someone online
Do not respond; block and report; tell a trusted adult
Stealing personal details to pretend to be you
Do not share Aadhaar/PAN copies carelessly
Malware that locks your files and demands money
Do not open unknown attachments; keep backups
Fake shopping sites, lottery scams, UPI fraud
Remember: you never need to enter your UPI PIN to receive money
Repeatedly following or monitoring someone online
Keep profiles private; report to police

blocks.html: In India, cybercrime can be reported at cybercrime.gov.in or by calling the national cyber helpline 1930.

items.html: Safe browsing: Visit only trusted websites; look for https:// and the padlock icon; avoid clicking pop-ups.
Identity protection: Do not share personal details with strangers; log out from shared computers.
Confidentiality: Use strong, different passwords; never write them where others can see them.
Malware protection: Use antivirus software; keep the OS and apps updated; scan pen drives.
Public Wi-Fi: Avoid online banking on public Wi-Fi.

blocks.html: Types of malware: virus (attaches to files and spreads), worm (spreads by itself over networks), Trojan (looks useful but is harmful), spyware (secretly records your activity), adware (shows unwanted ads), ransomware (locks files for ransom).
The IT Act, 2000 (amended in 2008) is India's main law for electronic transactions and cybercrime.

items.html: Gives legal recognition to electronic records and digital signatures.
Supports e-governance and e-commerce.
Defines cybercrimes and punishments, such as hacking, identity theft and publishing obscene material.
Set up the Cyber Appellate Tribunal to hear appeals (since 2017 this work is done by TDSAT).

blocks.html: E-waste is discarded electronic equipment: old phones, computers, chargers, batteries, TVs and printers. It contains harmful substances such as lead, mercury and cadmium that pollute soil and water and harm human health when burnt or dumped.

items.html: Reduce: Buy only what you need; use devices longer.
Reuse: Donate or sell working devices; repair instead of replacing.
Recycle: Give e-waste to authorised recyclers or company take-back programmes, not to the kabadiwala who burns wires.

blocks.html: India's E-Waste (Management) Rules make producers responsible for collecting and recycling their products (Extended Producer Responsibility).

rows: Looking at screens for long periods
Follow the 20-20-20 rule: every 20 minutes, look 20 feet away for 20 seconds
Sit straight; keep the screen at eye level (ergonomics)
Take breaks; use a proper keyboard position
Stop screens an hour before bed

items.html: Footprint check: Search your own name online (with a parent or teacher). Make a list of what you find and decide what you would like to remove.
Spot the phishing: Your teacher will show 5 messages. Identify which are phishing and list the warning signs (urgent tone, wrong spelling, unknown link, asking for OTP).
Password strength in C++: Write a program that rates a password as Weak, Medium or Strong based on length, digits, uppercase and special characters (use Chapter 8 skills).
Licence hunt: Find the licence of 5 software or apps you use (Help → About). Classify each as proprietary, GPL, Apache or other.
E-waste survey: Count the unused electronic items in your home. Find the nearest authorised e-waste collection centre in your city.
Poster: Make a poster on "Cyber Safety for School Students" with 8 rules.

blocks.html: 1. What is a digital footprint? Name its two types.

Answer: A digital footprint is the trail of data a person leaves while using the internet. Types: active (shared on purpose, e.g. posts) and passive (collected without knowledge, e.g. browsing history).
2. Differentiate between copyright and patent.

Answer: Copyright protects original creative works such as books, music and software code. A patent protects a new invention or process, giving the inventor the sole right to make and sell it for a fixed period.
3. What is plagiarism? How can it be avoided?
Answer: Plagiarism is using someone else's work or ideas without giving credit. It can be avoided by writing in your own words and citing the source of every idea or quotation.
4. Write any four net etiquettes.
Answer: Respect others' privacy; do not troll or bully; verify information before forwarding; respect copyright and do not post others' work as your own.
5. What is cyberbullying? What should a victim do?

Answer: Cyberbullying is harassing, threatening or insulting someone online. The victim should not respond, should block the person, keep screenshots as evidence, report it on the platform or at cybercrime.gov.in, and tell a trusted adult.
6. What is e-waste? Name two ways to manage it.
Answer: E-waste is discarded electronic equipment such as old phones and computers. It can be managed by reusing (donating working devices) and recycling through authorised recyclers.
7. Differentiate between a virus and a worm.
Answer: A virus attaches itself to a file and spreads when the file is opened or copied. A worm is a standalone program that copies and spreads itself over a network without any user action.
8. What is the Creative Commons licence?
Answer: A licence for creative content (images, text, music) that lets creators allow others to use their work under chosen conditions, such as giving credit (BY) or non- commercial use only (NC).
1. Explain any five cybercrimes and how to protect yourself from them.
Answer: See the table in 11.7: hacking, phishing, cyberbullying, identity theft, ransomware, online fraud and cyber stalking, with a safety measure for each.
2. Explain Intellectual Property Rights and the ways in which IPR can be violated.
Answer: See 11.5: copyright, patent and trademark (with examples), and violations — plagiarism, copyright infringement and trademark infringement.
3. What is e-waste? Why is it harmful? Explain the 3 Rs of e-waste management.

Answer: See 11.10. E-waste contains lead, mercury and cadmium, which pollute soil and water and damage health when burnt or dumped. Reduce (buy less, use longer), Reuse (donate, repair), Recycle (authorised recyclers, take-back schemes).
4. List five health problems caused by overuse of technology and their prevention.

Answer: See the table in 11.11: eye strain (20-20-20 rule), back and neck pain (good posture, ergonomics), wrist pain (breaks), sleep problems (no screens before bed), internet addiction (screen-time limits, outdoor play).

blocks.html: 1. (a) What is a software licence? Compare proprietary, GPL, Apache and Creative Commons licences. (6) (b) What is FOSS? Give four examples and two advantages. (4)
Answer (a): See the table in 11.6.

Answer (b): FOSS is software whose source code is freely available to run, study, change and share. Examples: Linux, LibreOffice, Firefox, GIMP, g++ . Advantages: free of cost; can be customised and improved by anyone; usually secure because many people review the code.
2. (a) Explain cyber safety measures: safe browsing, identity protection, confidentiality and malware protection. (6) (b) Write the main provisions of the IT Act, 2000. (4)
Answer (a): See 11.8.

Answer (b): See 11.9: legal recognition to electronic records and digital signatures; support for e-governance and e-commerce; definitions and penalties for cybercrimes; an appellate body for disputes. It was amended in 2008 to add more cybercrimes.
3. (a) Explain net etiquette, communication etiquette and social media etiquette. (6) (b) What is data protection? Write four ways to protect personal data. (4)
Answer (a): See 11.3.

Answer (b): See 11.4: strong unique passwords and two-factor authentication; share only necessary data; check app permissions; avoid public Wi-Fi for banking; India's DPDP Act, 2023 gives legal protection to personal data.
